question: How can the scattered literature on handling concept drift in online supervised learning be organised into one taxonomy of adaptive learning methods, evaluation methods and applications?
contributions: Characterise the adaptive learning process (predict, diagnose, update) and the types of drift (Sec 2).
Propose a taxonomy around four modules: memory, change detection, learning, loss estimation (Sec 3).
Discuss evaluation methodology for adaptive learners on streams (Sec 4).
Present illustrative applications and a collection of benchmark datasets and a MOA example (Sec 2.5, online appendices B and C).

results.claim: Real concept drift is a change in p(y|X); only changes that affect the prediction decision require adaptation; virtual drift is a change in p(X) alone.
results.setup: Definitions, Sec 2.1; formal drift is exists X: p_t0(X,y) != p_t1(X,y) (Eq 2).
results.quote: From a predictive perspective only the changes that affect the prediction decision require adaptation.

results.claim: Adaptive learning is a loop of predict, diagnose, update, built from memory, learning, change-detection and loss-estimation modules.
results.setup: Generic online adaptive learner, Fig 3 and Sec 2.4.
results.quote: Section 3 will discuss the four modules of the system (Data Management, Learning, Change Detection, Loss Estimation) in detail.

results.claim: Blind adaptation (fixed windows, example weighting, plain online learners) forgets old concepts at a constant speed whether or not drift happens; informed adaptation reacts to a detector trigger.
results.quote: The blind approaches forget old concepts at a constant speed independently of whether changes are happening or not.

results.claim: Detector memory and processing cost: sequential analysis and SPC are O(1); two-distribution monitoring such as ADWIN is O(log W) to O(W).
results.source: Table II of this survey (CUSUM, PH, SPC, ADWIN)
results.setup: W is the size of the detection window.
results.quote: Comparing two distributions for change detection requires more computational resources than detecting based on the evolution of indicators, but potentially may give more precise information about the location of change.

results.claim: ADWIN suggested default confidence parameter delta.
results.setup: ADWIN drops the older subwindow when two subwindow means differ by more than eps_cut = sqrt((1/2m) ln(4|W|/delta)), m the harmonic mean of the subwindow sizes.
results.quote: the suggested default value is 0.2

results.claim: SPC drift-detector thresholds: Warning at p_i + sigma_i >= p_min + 2*sigma_min (95%), Out-of-Control at >= p_min + 3*sigma_min (99%).
results.setup: Error rate treated as Binomial approximated by Normal, valid for n > 30 examples; the 3 is the Out-of-Control multiplier, 2 the Warning multiplier.
results.quote: pi + σi ≥pmin + 3 ∗σmin
results.note: Algorithm 3 in the appendix uses parameters alpha (out-control) and beta (warning) instead of the literals 3 and 2.

results.claim: Exponential ageing weight of an example that arrived j steps ago is exp(-lambda*j); lambda = 0 weights all examples equally.
results.setup: Gradual forgetting, full memory.
results.quote: If λ = 0, all the examples have the same weight.

results.claim: Reservoir sampling adds the i-th item with probability k/i, k the reservoir size.
results.setup: Sampling as an alternative to windows.
results.quote: When the ith item arrives, it is added to the reservoir with probability p = k/i

results.claim: Ensemble diversity: before a drift, low-diversity ensembles have lower test error; shortly after a drift, highly diverse ensembles are better regardless of drift type; long after, diversity matters less.
results.setup: Ensembles under different drift types.
results.quote: shortly after the drift occurs, highly diverse ensembles are better regardless the type of drift

results.claim: Weighted ensemble weight w_i = MSE_r - MSE_i, where MSE_r is the MSE of a random classifier.
results.setup: Classifiers trained on sequential stream batches.
results.quote: the weight wi of a classiﬁer Li is wi = MSEr −MSEi

results.claim: Cross-validation is not directly applicable to evolving streams because it mixes temporal order; use holdout, prequential (test-then-train) or controlled permutations.
results.setup: Evaluation, Sec 4.2.
results.quote: cross-validation is not directly applicable to the streaming settings with evolving data because it would mix the temporal order of data.

results.claim: McNemar test between two stream classifiers rejects equality at 0.99 confidence when M exceeds 6.635, M = sign(a-b)(a-b)^2/(a+b).
results.setup: a = instances misclassified by the first classifier only, b = by the second only.

results.claim: Nemenyi critical difference CD = q_alpha * sqrt(k(k+1)/6N) for k learners over N datasets, used after a Friedman rejection.
results.setup: Comparison of more than two classifiers.
results.quote: CD = qα

results.claim: MOA example: a prequential sliding window of size 1000 approximates hold-out evaluation on a stream of one million instances.
results.setup: MOA, one-million-instance stream; Fig 11 compares hold-out, prequential landmark and prequential sliding window.
results.quote: a prequential evaluation using a sliding window of size 1000
results.note: The accuracy curves are only in figures, not in the text.

results.claim: MOA drift experiment: Random RBF stream, centroids move at constant speed 1e-4 per instance; Hoeffding Tree adapts least, ensembles do better but cost more RAM-Hours, Leveraging Bagging scores highest accuracy and Kappa at the highest resource cost.
results.setup: Random RBF generator, one million instances, prequential sliding window 1000; learners Hoeffding Tree, Adaptive Hoeffding Tree, ADWIN Bagging, Leveraging Bagging.
results.quote: constant speed 10−4
results.note: Fig 12 accuracy, Kappa and RAM-Hours values are not in the text.

results.claim: RAM-Hour: every GB of RAM deployed for 1 hour equals one RAM-Hour, a cost measure based on cloud rental.
results.setup: Streaming resource measure.
results.quote: Every GB of RAM deployed for 1 hour equals one RAM-Hour.

results.claim: ELEC2 electricity dataset has 45,312 instances, one per 30 minutes (48 per day); label is price change relative to a 24-hour moving average.
results.setup: Australian New South Wales Electricity Market.
results.quote: The ELEC2 dataset contains 45, 312

results.claim: Airline dataset holds about 116 million flight records.
results.setup: Real-world concept-drift data.
results.quote: approximately 116 million

results.claim: LED generator optimal Bayes accuracy is 74% with each attribute inverted with 10% chance; waveform optimal Bayes accuracy is 86%.
results.setup: LED seven-segment digit task; waveform is 3 classes, wave21 with 21 attributes, wave40 with 19 added irrelevant ones.
results.quote: accuracy is 74%

results.claim: SEA generator concepts use boundary x1 + x2 <= theta with theta = 9, 8, 7, 9.5 over three attributes in [0,10], only two relevant.
results.setup: Four abrupt concepts.

results.claim: The Netflix rating matrix is high-dimensional and about 1% non-zero, so windowing and instance weighting are not the best choice for collaborative filtering drift.
results.setup: Netflix Prize, winning ensemble handled many kinds of change.
results.quote: containing only about 1% of non-zero elements

results.claim: Data volume generated in 2012 was estimated to surpass 2.8 zetabytes.
results.setup: Motivation for stream mining.
results.quote: surpass 2.8 zetabytes

limits: Covers only real concept drift in online supervised learning with immediate labels; drifting priors, novelty detection and semi-supervised clustering-based methods are excluded (Sec 2.1).
The authors concede that most methods do not address representation bias in closed-loop systems, so historical replay cannot validate them (Sec 5).
Delayed or on-demand labels and unsupervised drift handling were only beginning to be studied (Sec 5).
Predates deep learning and ML-platform monitoring; the methods are classical stream learners (Hoeffding trees, ensembles, ADWIN, SPC).
The PDF is a pre-publication version: the volume, DOI and 2014 date are not confirmed in it; some citations print as [?] (STAGGER in App B).
The only experiments are the MOA illustration in App C, with results only in figures.
practices: Do not mistake outliers or noise for drift; the learner must be adaptive yet robust to noise (Sec 2.2-2.3).
Understand the nature and source of drift first, then engineer the adaptive strategy (Sec 2.5.4).
Use a naive baseline such as 'tomorrow will look the same like today' to judge the gain of an adaptive method (Sec 4.1).
Evaluate change detectors on true detection probability, false alarm rate or average run length, detection delay and detection-point accuracy; count false alarms only on drift-free data (Sec 4.1).
Use prequential evaluation (test-then-train) with a sliding window or fading factor instead of cross-validation (Sec 4.2.1).
Use controlled permutations to avoid overfitting to one fixed stream order (Sec 4.2.1).
Report cost with RAM-Hours and use the Kappa statistic for imbalanced streams (Sec 4.1).
Test significance with McNemar for two classifiers and Friedman then Nemenyi for several (Sec 4.2.3).
Use synthetic streams for known drift ground truth and real streams for realism (Sec 4.3, App B).
Choose window size by the trade-off: short windows adapt fast but hurt in stable periods (Sec 3.1.1).

terms.definition: Formally between t0 and t1: exists X such that p_t0(X,y) != p_t1(X,y).
Changes in p(y|X), with or without change in p(X).
Change in the data distribution p(X) without affecting p(y|X).
Changes in the population from which future samples will be drawn compared with the design sample.
Sudden/abrupt, incremental, gradual, reoccurring concepts; an outlier is not drift.
Incremental algorithm that may access previous or selected examples.
Blind adapts without explicit change detection; informed reacts to a trigger such as a change detector.
Interleaved test-then-train: each instance tests the model before it is used for training; error is the accumulated sum of a loss S = sum f(y_hat_t, y_t).
The balance between being stable to handle noise and learning new patterns when learning continuously from a stream.
Some neural networks completely forget past patterns when exposed to a new set of patterns.
One GB of RAM deployed for one hour.
Sequential tests: g_t = max(0, g_{t-1} + (x_t - delta)) alarmed when above lambda; PH uses m_T minus its running minimum M_T against lambda.

In-Control: p_j + s_j < p_min + 2*s_min; Out-of-Control: p_j + s_j >= p_min + 3*s_min; Warning in between
Z_0 = mu_0, Z_t = (1 - lambda) Z_{t-1} + lambda e_t; signal change when Z_t > mu_0 + L sigma_Zt (EWMA)
